I'll start by reading the workflow-relevant files, then orchestrate a multi-agent scrutiny pass.

1	# AGENTS
2	
3	Next.js 16 App Router + Prisma/PostgreSQL + NextAuth. TypeScript strict, Tailwind, shadcn/ui.
4	
5	These instructions govern all feature, fix, refactor, documentation, and
6	maintenance work in this repository. All agents and sub-agents must follow them.
7	
8	## Commands
9	
10	```bash
11	npm ci                      # Node 22 required (.npmrc engine-strict blocks other majors)
12	npm run dev                 # http://localhost:3000
13	npm run lint                # eslint app components lib
14	npx tsc --noEmit            # typecheck (no npm script)
15	npm test                    # Jest, both projects — needs a running Postgres (see Gotchas)
16	npm run test:unit -- --testPathPattern flightTime   # one file; see Gotchas before using a bare path
17	npm run test:database       # the *.database.test.ts project, serialised
18	npx playwright test         # E2E; starts its own dev server, so free port 3000 first
19	npm run build               # next build + scripts/sanitize-standalone.mjs
20	```
21	
22	```bash
23	docker compose up --build         # full stack: db + mailpit + proxy, migrates and seeds
24	docker compose up -d db mailpit   # just the services Jest and Playwright need
25	npx prisma migrate deploy && npx prisma db seed
26	```
27	
28	## Environment
29	
30	`cp .env.example .env`, then generate three secrets:
31	
32	- `NEXTAUTH_SECRET` — 32+ characters
33	- `PASSENGER_DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEYS` — `local-v1:$(openssl rand -base64 32)`
34	- `STAFF_MFA_ENCRYPTION_KEYS` — a *different* `local-v1:$(openssl rand -base64 32)`
35	
36	`lib/env.ts` validates all eight required variables fail-closed at boot (via
37	`instrumentation.ts`). A malformed key ring crashes startup rather than degrading.
38	
39	`.env.example` also carries `DATABASE_IS_DISPOSABLE=true`. A Playwright run and the
40	database Jest project delete every booking in the database they are pointed at, and
41	refuse to start without it — host and name cannot tell a developer's database from a
42	deployment, since Compose gives the application the same pair. Never set it where
43	this application is deployed.
44	
45	Local verification and recovery email lands in Mailpit at http://localhost:8025.
46	
47	Never commit a secret value or pass one on the command line. Every environment
48	that runs this application injects configuration at runtime.
49	
50	## Architecture
51	
52	- `app/actions.ts` — `'use server'`; the primary mutation path for the whole app
53	- `app/api/` — auth routes only (register, verify, password reset, NextAuth)
54	- `lib/*Service.ts` — data and business logic, called from server actions
55	- `lib/validation.ts` — shared Zod schemas; mutations parse through `parseActionInput`
56	- `lib/actionResult.ts` — mutations return `{ ok: false, error }` instead of throwing on validation failure
57	- `prisma/schema.prisma` — migrations are hand-authored SQL, several security-critical
58	
59	## Gotchas
60	
61	- A migration that fails leaves Prisma refusing to apply anything else: the next
62	  `migrate deploy` reports `P3009`, not the original error. Fix the data the migration
63	  objected to, then `npx prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back <migration_name>` before
64	  deploying again. A failed migration rolls back whole — no half-created type or
65	  column survives — so the retry is clean. Several migrations here `RAISE EXCEPTION`
66	  deliberately rather than let a cast fail with a less useful message, so this is a
67	  normal path rather than a disaster
68	- There are no down migrations. Rolling one back means reversing its SQL by hand and
69	  deleting its row from `_prisma_migrations`; write the reversal in the migration's
70	  header comment when it is not obvious
71	- `__tests__/**/*.database.test.ts` require a live Postgres; start it before `npm test`
72	- Those files run serially in their own Jest project: they share one database and
73	  several assert against whole tables, so running them beside each other counted one
74	  file's fixtures in another file's scan (#155). `npm test` runs the unit project
75	  first and stops if it fails, so pass flags to `test:unit`/`test:database` directly
76	  rather than to `npm test`, which does not forward them. What serialises them is
77	  `--runInBand` in the `test:database` script, not the config, so the project's
78	  `globalSetup` refuses any run it is not given — `npx jest --selectProjects
79	  database` stops with a message naming the worker count rather than
80	  reproducing the interference the split removed (#215)
81	- `npm run test:unit -- <path>` does **not** filter: it runs all of them and says nothing.
82	  The script ends in `--selectProjects unit`, which takes a list, so the path is read as
83	  another project name and ignored. Filter with `-- --testPathPattern <regex>` or
84	  `-- -t '<test name>'`. `npm run test:database -- <path>` does filter, because
85	  `--runInBand` sits between the project list and the path — which is exactly why the
86	  difference is easy to miss
87	- Node-environment tests need `/** @jest-environment node */` (jsdom is the Jest default)
88	- Playwright runs `workers: 1, fullyParallel: false` on purpose — parallel runs collide on the DB
89	- A Playwright run fails in `global-teardown` if it left accounts, tokens, reviews,
90	  favorites, notifications, flights or schedules behind. `global-setup` cannot delete
91	  those — it cannot tell a run's account from a developer's — so each spec deletes what
92	  it created in a `test.afterAll`, and the teardown compares snapshots to catch the ones
93	  that do not (#213). Two things trip it that are not a leak: a failing or interrupted
94	  test, whose `afterAll` never finished, and anything else writing to the same database
95	  during the run. Fix the failure, or run the suite alone, rather than the report
96	- Always `npm run build`, never bare `next build`: the sanitize step strips `.env` files from
97	  standalone output, and CI asserts no secret survives in any image layer
98	- Staff mutations gate on `hasVerifiedStaffAccess(session)` — a session alone is not enough;
99	  staff must complete TOTP enrollment (`docs/STAFF_ACCOUNT_POLICY.md`)
100	
101	## Code Style
102	
103	4-space indent, single quotes, semicolons. The `@/*` path alias maps to the repo root.
104	Chart and other browser-interactive components need `'use client'`.
105	
106	## Development Workflow
107	
108	1. **Inspect before changing anything.** Inspect the repository, current Git
109	   state, and all applicable instruction files before making changes. Preserve
110	   unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked work.
111	
112	2. **Create a branch first.** Create a dedicated feature, fix, refactor, chore,
113	   test, or documentation branch before making code changes. Never commit
114	   directly to `main`, and create the branch from the latest appropriate
115	   `main` state.
116	
117	3. **Choose a thin vertical slice.** Before implementing a tracked issue or
118	   feature, define the smallest end-to-end slice that can be reviewed, tested,
119	   shipped, and merged independently. Prefer one coherent user-visible or
120	   operational outcome over a broad horizontal layer. If the next issue is too
121	   large for one pull request, split it into ordered slices and complete only
122	   the current slice. Keep pull requests small enough for thorough review,
123	   reliable verification, and quick rollback. When work surfaces a defect or
124	   improvement that belongs outside the current slice, do not widen the slice
125	   to absorb it — file it as described under Issue Tracking and carry on.
126	
127	4. **Use test-driven development when behavior or structure is testable.**
128	   - Add or update a focused test before implementation.
129	   - Run it and confirm it fails for the expected reason.
130	   - Implement the smallest appropriate change.
131	   - Run focused tests while iterating.
132	   - Refactor only while the relevant tests remain green.
133	
134	5. **Inspect the complete diff.** Review the branch diff plus all staged,
135	   unstaged, and untracked files. Remove accidental or unrelated changes while
136	   preserving work that belongs to the user.
137	
138	6. **Run `ui-review` before verification.** After the main agent completes an
139	   implementation pass, invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent. The `ui-review`
140	   sub-agent must act as an expert in website design, usability,
141	   responsiveness, and accessibility. Address every actionable finding before
142	   running the `verifier`. For UI-affecting changes, exercise the changed
143	   journey in the rendered application at representative phone, tablet, and
144	   desktop viewports; inspect interaction, loading, empty, error, focus,
145	   keyboard, contrast, and responsive states as applicable; and capture
146	   screenshots or equivalent visual evidence. For changes with no UI impact,
147	   explicitly record that rendered UI review is not applicable. If a finding
148	   is not applicable, record the concrete reason rather than silently ignoring
149	   it.
150	
151	7. **Run `verifier` before code review.** Invoke the `verifier` sub-agent to run
152	   the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for the
153	   change. The verifier must report failures, flakes, missing coverage, and
154	   environment issues. Fix or explicitly resolve every actionable finding
155	   before starting code review. If a verifier finding requires a code change,
156	   rerun the focused tests for that change and then rerun the verifier — not
157	   the whole battery again.
158	
159	   **The verifier owns the slow checks; do not run them twice.** Split it by
160	   what a check costs:
161	
162	   | Main agent | Verifier |
163	   | --- | --- |
164	   | The TDD inner loop — one file, via `--testPathPattern` | The full unit *and* database projects |
165	   | The **red** step: does it fail for the intended reason | `npm run build` |
166	   | The whole unit project once a slice is done | The full `npx playwright test` |
167	   | `npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit` | Migrations against a fresh *and* a populated database |
168	   | The database tests covering what changed | An audit of every mutant reported killed, and of the selection |
169	   | The single Playwright spec whose journey changed | `npm run lint` and `npx tsc --noEmit` again, on the final tree |
170	
171	   The verifier's column costs minutes per entry. Running those in both places
172	   doubles every slice for no extra signal, and a second concurrent run competes
173	   for port 3000 and the shared database — which has already produced failures
174	   that looked real and were not. The cheap checks are the deliberate exception
175	   to the heading, and appear in both columns: lint, the typecheck and the unit
176	   project cost seconds, and the verifier's report is an independent statement
177	   about the final state rather than a summary of what it was told.
178	
179	   Two things cannot move to the verifier. **The red step is a design check, not
180	   a verification**: "does this fail for the reason I intended" needs the intent
181	   behind the test, so a sub-agent cannot answer it. And **fixing findings is
182	   always the main agent's**, which is the expensive half and the reason the
183	   rules below matter more than the split.
184	
185	   **Mutation testing is the main agent's**, and stays focused: run the suite
186	   that should catch the mutant, not everything. The verifier does not re-run
187	   it — it is barred from changing anything `git status` would report, because a
188	   sub-agent that injects a defect leaves one behind whenever a run is
189	   interrupted. It audits the claim instead, which means the claim has to reach
190	   it: **name each mutant and the suite that caught it when invoking the
191	   verifier.** An unreported mutant is an
192	   unaudited one, silently. Three that survived 781 tests reached a pull request
193	   this way (#231).
194	
195	   **Choose mutants to defeat the assertion, not to confirm it.** For each one,
196	   ask *what edit would leave this test green while making it meaningless*, and
197	   run that. Corrupting a value the assertion reads only proves the matcher
198	   works. Deleting the thing it claims to pin proves it is anchored to it — so
199	   for a guard over a table or a document, delete the row or the section, do not
200	   alter a word inside it.
201	
202	   Four guards written in one slice (#248) passed while asserting nothing, and
203	   every one looked rigorous:
204	
205	   - a line limit of 16 on an 11-line file, which left room for four lines of
206	     the instructions it existed to forbid
207	   - the same limit tightened to 11, which caught appends and still admitted a
208	     countermand of equal length, because counting lines cannot tell a pointer
209	     from its opposite
210	   - a check asking whether a document said `no Write`, against a document that
211	     says `no Edit or Write tool`, so it never armed
212	   - `expect(granted).toEqual(expect.not.arrayContaining([...]))`, a superset
213	     check that fails only when *every* barred item is present, so granting one
214	     walked past
215	
216	   The confirming mutants died in all four cases and reported nothing wrong. A
217	   table in which every mutant died is not weaker evidence than one containing a
218	   survivor — it is *more ambiguous*. It is equally consistent with a strong
219	   suite well attacked and with a weak one never attacked, and the table alone
220	   cannot separate them. So when everything dies on the first attempt, check the
221	   selection before concluding anything about the suite.
222	
223	   A survivor is a diagnostic, never a target. Producing one on demand is
224	   trivial — pick a throwaway mutant, or leave an assertion slightly loose — and
225	   a table padded that way is noise dressed as rigor.
226	
227	   The table lists *runs*, so it understates what the verifier is for. The
228	   verifier also classifies every failure as regression, pre-existing or
229	   environment, and cannot do that without knowing what was already red before
230	   the branch. **Say what is failing on `main`** when invoking it, or the
231	   classification is a guess dressed as a result.
232	
233	   The sub-agents' instructions live in `docs/VERIFIER.md` and `docs/UI_REVIEW.md`.
234	   The definitions under `.claude/agents/` are pointers at them and carry no
235	   rules, because a definition is injected into a sub-agent's context when the
236	   session first spawns it and is never refreshed: four verifier runs in one
237	   session followed instructions deleted two rounds earlier (#246). Edit the
238	   files in `docs/`. A sub-agent still cannot see that its *own* pointer or
239	   toolset changed mid-session, so **say so in the invocation** when a slice
240	   touches `.claude/agents/`.
241	
242	   **Running tests is not what fills the context window; unfiltered output is.**
243	   A whole unit run reduced to `| grep -E '^Tests:'` costs about fifty tokens for
244	   seven hundred tests, so the split above is about wall clock and contention,
245	   not context. Three habits protect context far more than it does:
246	
247	   - **Never launch the verifier until the tree is settled.** It reads from disk
248	     throughout rather than snapshotting, so an edit underneath it does not make
249	     the report stale — it makes it *incoherent*: early checks ran against one
250	     tree and later ones against another, and nothing marks where the boundary
251	     fell. The result certifies a state that never existed at any single moment.
252	     Wasted on both sides, twice in one session.
253	   - **Prefer one thorough pass to several narrow ones.** Batch the fixes for a
254	     round of findings and re-verify once. Passes that exist only because the
255	     previous round's fixes need re-checking are the ones worth designing out.
256	   - **Cap failure triage at two rounds.** Grep to the assertion and its
257	     expected/received before reading anything else. If two rounds do not
258	     explain the failure, hand the investigation to a sub-agent rather than
259	     reading progressively more output. The same goes for a failure that smells
260	     environmental — a stale `.next`, a port collision, a Prisma client left
261	     over from a branch switch: ask a sub-agent whether it is real.
262	
263	8. **Review the code before every commit.** Two mechanisms cover this, and
264	   neither is a bespoke sub-agent:
265	   - The `PreToolUse` hooks in `.claude/settings.json` review the diff
266	     automatically and block on `git push` and `gh pr create`. They run
267	     without being asked; do not work around a block by pushing differently.
268	   - `/code-review` gives a fuller pass, and against a pull request it runs
269	     unattended and posts its findings as a comment. It ships in the
270	     `code-review@claude-plugins-official` plugin rather than being built in,
271	     and this repository does not enable it, so it exists only where someone
272	     has installed it themselves — check before relying on it.
273	     `/code-review ultra` is deeper still, but it is user-triggered and
274	     billed, and an agent cannot launch it.
275	
276	   Nothing reviews the pull request afterwards, so this pass is the review
277	   rather than a first draft of one.
278	
279	   Reviewers must act as experts in the languages and frameworks used by this
280	   application, including TypeScript, React, Next.js, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Jest,
281	   and Playwright. Address every actionable finding before committing. If review
282	   findings cause changes, rerun the appropriate tests and the `verifier`, then
283	   obtain fresh review approval for the changed state.
284	
285	9. **Commit after approval.** Commit only after verification and code review
286	   are complete. Use Conventional Commits:
287	
288	   ```text
289	   <type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>
290	   ```
291	
292	   Keep the subject at 72 characters or fewer, describe why in the body when
293	   useful, and do not combine unrelated work.
294	
295	10. **Create pull requests from the reviewed state.**
296	    - Confirm that local verification remains valid.
297	    - Rerun code review only if the reviewed state changed after the pre-commit
298	      review.
299	    - A changed state includes code, tests, documentation, generated files,
300	      conflict resolution, or any other staged, unstaged, or untracked content.
301	    - Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and worktree
302	      remain unchanged.
303	    - Push and create the pull request only after local verification and any
304	      required code review are complete.
305	    - Open a normal, ready-for-review pull request by default. Do not open draft
306	      pull requests unless the user explicitly asks for a draft.
307	
308	11. **Answer whatever review the pull request attracts.** No automated
309	    reviewer gates a merge here. Where a human or a bot does leave findings,
310	    address them, re-run steps 6 to 9 for whatever changed, push, and reply
311	    saying what changed — and where a finding is right about the problem but
312	    wrong about the fix, say so rather than resolving it quietly.
313	
314	12. **Merge only clean, passing pull requests.** Merge only after GitHub
315	    reports a clean merge state, every configured check passes, and no review
316	    thread is left unresolved. Never bypass a failing or pending required
317	    check. Self-merges are allowed when these conditions are met. Use squash
318	    merge for short-lived development branches to keep `main` linear, then
319	    delete the merged branch.
320	
321	## Testing Expectations
322	
323	- Preserve all existing tests and add coverage for new behavior and
324	  regressions.
325	- Add functional coverage for complete user journeys when a change crosses
326	  component, server, database, or authentication boundaries.
327	- Use Jest and Testing Library for focused unit/component/integration tests and
328	  Playwright for browser journeys.
329	- Mock true external boundaries in focused tests; use realistic local services
330	  for end-to-end verification where appropriate.
331	- Treat warnings, flakes, skipped checks, and environment failures as findings
332	  that require an explicit resolution.
333	
334	## Issue Tracking
335	
336	- GitHub issues labelled `roadmap` are the source of truth for product
337	  hardening work. The `Phase 1` through `Phase 5` milestones carry the priority
338	  order; work phases in order unless a later item is an explicit prerequisite
339	  for current work.
340	- Reference the issue number in the pull request. When a pull request delivers
341	  only part of an issue, comment with the number and what remains rather than
342	  closing it.
343	- **File anything found but not fixed.** When work surfaces a defect, risk, or
344	  improvement outside the current slice, open a GitHub issue for it before
345	  moving on. A finding recorded only in a commit message, a pull request
346	  comment, or a chat reply is a finding that gets lost. Search open issues
347	  first and comment on the existing one instead of opening a duplicate.
348	- An issue filed this way states where the problem is (file and line), what
349	  was observed, and why it matters. Say whether it was verified against
350	  running code or is a reading of the source that still needs confirming.
351	  Apply `roadmap` only when it is product-hardening work belonging to a phase.
352	- Filing is not a substitute for finishing the current slice. If the finding
353	  makes the slice wrong or unsafe to ship, say so and stop instead of filing
354	  around it.
355	
356	## Containerization Fallback
357	
358	- Docker and Docker Compose are preferred when available.
359	- If Docker or Docker Compose is unavailable or fails because this machine uses
360	  Podman, fall back to `podman` and `podman-compose` respectively.
361

67	
68	```bash
69	docker compose up -d db mailpit          # podman/podman-compose if Docker is absent
70	npx prisma migrate deploy && npx prisma db seed
71	```
72	
73	Create a scratch database and run `migrate deploy` against it. Then run it
74	against a *populated* one as well: a migration that backfills or converts data
75	is trivially correct against zero rows, and the guards in this repository exist
76	precisely because real rows fail them. If a migration carries a guard, exercise
77	it in both directions — make it fire, then make it pass — rather than trusting
78	that it would work.
79	
80	## Environment traps that produce false results
81	
82	- Jest and Playwright need Postgres up; `*.database.test.ts` fail without it
83	- After a schema change, run `npx prisma generate`, then **delete `.next`**.
84	  A stale build bundles the old Prisma client, and the failure it produces
85	  looks like an application bug ("Argument `x` is missing") rather than a
86	  cache artifact.
87	- A stale dev server holding port 3000 makes Playwright time out on startup
88	- Playwright runs `workers: 1, fullyParallel: false` on purpose; do not
89	  parallelise it
90	- `npm run test:unit -- <path>` does **not** filter. The script ends in
91	  `--selectProjects unit`, which takes a list, so the path is read as another
92	  project name and ignored: you get the whole project and no warning. Re-running one
93	  suite in isolation needs `-- --testPathPattern <regex>` or `-- -t '<name>'`
94	- `npx jest --selectProjects database` aborts by design. `jest.database-setup.js`
95	  refuses to start when it sees more than one worker, because those tests share
96	  one database. Use `npm run test:database`, which passes `--runInBand` — and
97	  unlike the unit script, that one *does* forward a trailing path
98	
99	## Flakes are findings
100	
101	A test that passes on retry has not passed. When something fails:
102	
103	1. Determine whether it fails for a reason connected to the diff
104	2. Re-run it in isolation and as part of the suite — order-dependence and
105	   cold-start timing are common here
106	3. Report the mechanism, not just "flaky"
107	
108	**Cap this at three full-suite runs.** You cannot delegate — you have no Task
109	tool — so the bound has to be self-imposed, and characterising a rate precisely
110	is worth far less than reporting it roughly and moving on. "Failed twice in
111	three runs, always on the same assertion, here is the line" is a finding. Ten
112	runs to establish it was 1-in-5 is a finding plus nine runs of nothing.
113	
114	Distinguish clearly between: a real regression from this change, a pre-existing
115	failure the change merely surfaced, and an environment problem. Getting this
116	wrong wastes the most time of anything you do.
117	
118	## Coverage
119	
120	Note behaviour the change introduces that no test would catch. Call out
121	assertions that pass vacuously — a mocked return that omits the field under
122	test, an assertion the code path never reaches because an earlier error is
123	swallowed. A green suite that never exercises the change is a finding.
124	
125	Where the main agent reports having killed a mutant, audit the claim rather
126	than taking it — **from the source, without reproducing it**, per the rule at
127	the top of this file. Read the test it named: does an assertion actually
128	constrain the mutated value, or does the suite merely execute the line? A mocked
129	return that omits the field, an expectation on a wrapper object that would hold
130	for any payload, and an assertion after an early return all read as coverage and
131	constrain nothing.
132	
133	Audit the *selection* as well as each claim. A table in which every mutant died
134	on the first attempt is not weaker than one containing a survivor, but it is
135	more ambiguous: it may mean the assertions hold, or that only confirming mutants
136	were tried, and the table cannot tell you which. Ask what
137	edit would leave the test green while making it meaningless — a limit with
138	headroom, a matcher that checks a superset, a string search that never matches
139	the wording it is aimed at — and say when the reported mutants would not have
140	found it. Four such guards shipped past their own mutant tables in one slice
141	(#248).
142	
143	Do not report the absence of a survivor as a finding in itself. A survivor is a
144	diagnostic, not a quota, and treating it as one buys padded tables rather than
145	better selection.
146	
147	Mutants reported dead that were alive have reached a pull request here (#231):
148	three of them — two dropped `set_config` calls and a hard-coded zero — passed
149	all 781 tests. Say when a claim is not auditable from the source rather than
150	passing it, and check the count as well as the kill, since a "two suites went
151	red" that was really one is the same reporting error in miniature.
152	
153	**Silence is also a finding.** A change to behaviour that arrives with no mutant
154	named at all is not evidence that none was warranted — the main agent is
155	required to name them, so nothing reported means either nothing was done or
156	nothing was passed on. You cannot tell which from here and cannot ask: there is
157	no channel back mid-run. Report it as a coverage finding and say which behaviour
158	you would have expected a mutant for.
159	
160	## Report
161	
162	State what you ran, the actual result of each, and the exact output for
163	anything that failed. Then list findings, most severe first, each marked as
164	regression / pre-existing / environment / coverage gap.
165	
166	Never report success you did not observe. If you could not run something, say
167	which and why — an unrun check is not a passing one.
168

1	# UI review
2	
3	The instructions for the `ui-review` sub-agent. Its definition at
4	`.claude/agents/ui-review.md` is a pointer at this file: a definition is injected
5	once per session and goes stale, this is read fresh on every run (#246).
6	
7	You are an expert in website design, usability, responsiveness and accessibility,
8	reviewing a change to Mona Airways (Next.js App Router, Tailwind, shadcn/ui).
9	
10	You review. You do not fix: you have no editing tools, and that is deliberate.
11	Report findings and let the main agent act on them.
12	
13	Read `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, this file, and `AGENTS.md` from disk when
14	reasoning about them. What was injected into your context is a snapshot from
15	when the session first spawned you and is never refreshed, so it can lag the
16	worktree you are reviewing. If the copy of this role in your context holds
17	inline instructions rather than a pointer, it predates the split (#246) and
18	everything in it may be stale; the pointer on disk names where the current
19	version lives. Read it before trusting anything you were given.
20	
21	## Read the change first
22	
23	Establish what actually changed before opening a browser:
24	
25	- `git diff main...HEAD` plus staged, unstaged and untracked files
26	- Which routes, components and user journeys those files affect
27	
28	If nothing in the diff can alter rendered output — server-only logic, tests,
29	migrations, tooling — say so explicitly, state why, and stop. "Rendered UI
30	review is not applicable because X" is a complete and valid result. Do not
31	invent UI concerns to justify the invocation.
32	
33	## Exercise the real application
34	
35	For anything that does affect rendered output, look at it running. Reading JSX
36	is not review: a component can be correct in isolation and still render the
37	wrong thing once real data reaches it.
38	
39	Start the app if it is not already up (`npm run dev`, http://localhost:3000).
40	Drive the changed journey end to end at three viewports:
41	
42	- phone, 390x844
43	- tablet, 768x1024
44	- desktop, 1440x900
45	
46	Capture a screenshot at each. Inspect whichever of these the change can reach:
47	interaction, loading, empty, error, focus, keyboard, contrast, and responsive
48	states.
49	
50	Prefer the seeded local data over contrived fixtures. Several defects in this
51	codebase were invisible to component tests and obvious the moment a real
52	round-trip booking was rendered.
53	
54	## What to look for
55	
56	- **Does it say the true thing?** A card that names one flight while listing
57	  another leg's data is a defect even when every element renders correctly.
58	- Layout at every width; the page body must never scroll horizontally
59	- Keyboard reachability, visible focus, logical tab order, focus restoration
60	  after dialogs close
61	- Accessible names and roles; anything conveyed only by colour or position
62	- Contrast against the dark theme this app uses
63	- Loading, empty and error states, not just the happy path
64	- Console errors and React warnings during the journey
65	
66	## Report
67	
68	Return a list of findings, most severe first. For each: what is wrong, where
69	(`file:line` when you can place it), which viewport and state you saw it in,
70	and what the user experiences as a result. Reference the screenshots you took.
71	
72	Separate blocking defects from suggestions, and say plainly when a heading has
73	nothing to report. If a finding does not apply, record the concrete reason
74	rather than dropping it silently.
75	
76	State honestly what you could not exercise and why — a journey you could not
77	reach is a gap in the review, not a pass.
78

input.script:
export const meta = {
  name: 'scrutinize-agents-workflow',
  description: 'Scrutinize AGENTS.md development workflow and sub-agent definitions for gaps, contradictions and unowned checks',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Analyze', detail: 'four independent lenses over the workflow and sub-agents' },
    { title: 'Refute', detail: 'adversarial verification of each candidate finding' },
    { title: 'Synthesize', detail: 'rank survivors and propose concrete edits' },
  ],
}

const ROOT = '/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app'

const CONTEXT = `
Repository: ${ROOT} (Mona Airways, Next.js 16 + Prisma + NextAuth).

Read these files from disk before concluding anything:
- ${ROOT}/AGENTS.md  (the whole agent rulebook; "## Development Workflow" steps 1-12 are the subject)
- ${ROOT}/CLAUDE.md
- ${ROOT}/.claude/agents/verifier.md
- ${ROOT}/.claude/agents/ui-review.md
- ${ROOT}/.claude/agents/entire-search.md
- ${ROOT}/docs/VERIFIER.md
- ${ROOT}/docs/UI_REVIEW.md
- ${ROOT}/.claude/settings.json  (hooks referenced by step 8)
- ${ROOT}/__tests__/docs/agentInstructions.test.ts  (the guard over all of the above)
- ${ROOT}/package.json  (the scripts the workflow names)

Ground truth about how Claude Code actually resolves sub-agents, which you may
rely on:
- A sub-agent definition file in .claude/agents/ has YAML frontmatter with
  name / description / tools / model. The 'tools' line is an allowlist; omitting
  it inherits every tool.
- The ONLY sub-agent types registered in this session are, verbatim from the
  runtime registry: claude, claude-code-guide, several claude-security:* agents,
  code-simplifier, entire-search, Explore, general-purpose, Plan,
  statusline-setup, ui-review, verifier.
- 'ui-review' is registered with tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, and the
  mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_* tools (navigate, navigate_back,
  snapshot, take_screenshot, resize, click, type, fill_form, press_key, hover,
  select_option, evaluate, console_messages, wait_for, find, tabs, close).
- 'verifier' is registered with tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash.
- The Playwright browser tools come from a PLUGIN MCP server
  (mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__*), i.e. they exist only where that plugin
  is installed; they are not built in to this repository.
- '/code-review' ships in the code-review@claude-plugins-official plugin.

Be concrete and evidence-based. Quote the exact line you are indicting with a
file:line reference. Do not invent problems to fill a quota; a dimension with
nothing real to report should say so.
`

const FINDINGS_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    findings: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          title: { type: 'string', description: 'One-line claim' },
          location: { type: 'string', description: 'file:line or file:section' },
          evidence: { type: 'string', description: 'Exact quoted text plus why it is wrong' },
          impact: { type: 'string', description: 'What goes wrong in practice for an agent following this' },
          severity: { type: 'string', enum: ['blocking', 'high', 'medium', 'low'] },
          proposed_fix: { type: 'string', description: 'Concrete edit: what text to change to what' },
        },
        required: ['title', 'location', 'evidence', 'impact', 'severity', 'proposed_fix'],
      },
    },
  },
  required: ['findings'],
}

const VERDICT_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    refuted: { type: 'boolean', description: 'true if the finding is wrong, already handled elsewhere, or not actionable' },
    reason: { type: 'string' },
    corrected_claim: { type: 'string', description: 'If the finding is right about a problem but wrong about details, the accurate version' },
    corrected_fix: { type: 'string', description: 'The fix you would actually make, if it differs from the proposed one' },
  },
  required: ['refuted', 'reason'],
}

const DIMENSIONS = [
  {
    key: 'subagent-fidelity',
    prompt: `${CONTEXT}

LENS: sub-agent fidelity. Does each sub-agent definition, its instruction doc,
and the runtime registry agree with one another and with reality?

Check specifically:
- Every claim a doc in docs/ makes about its own toolset, against the tools
  actually granted in .claude/agents/*.md and in the registry above. A doc that
  says "you have no editing tools" while the agent holds Bash is asserting
  something false. Note how docs/VERIFIER.md handles this versus docs/UI_REVIEW.md.
- Whether the tools each agent IS granted suffice for what its doc orders it to
  do. e.g. docs/UI_REVIEW.md orders "Start the app if it is not already up
  (npm run dev)" and screenshots at three viewports; docs/VERIFIER.md orders
  scratch-database creation and 'delete .next'. Trace each ordered action to a
  granted tool.
- The Playwright browser tools ui-review depends on come from an optional
  plugin. What happens to step 6 of the workflow on a machine without it? Does
  any file say?
- .claude/agents/entire-search.md exists and is referenced by nothing in
  AGENTS.md or the guard test. Is that a gap, benign, or correctly excluded?
- The frontmatter 'description' fields: do they route correctly, i.e. would an
  agent reading only the registry know when to spawn each?
- Anything in docs/ that instructs the sub-agent to do something it is
  structurally unable to do (ask a question, delegate, be re-invoked mid-run).

Report only defects you can evidence.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'workflow-steps',
    prompt: `${CONTEXT}

LENS: the twelve Development Workflow steps as an executable procedure. Walk
them in order as if you were an agent about to implement a small slice, and find
where the procedure is ambiguous, circular, unsatisfiable, or silently optional.

Check specifically:
- Step 6 -> 7 -> 8 -> 9 -> 10 -> 11 -> 12 as a control flow. What happens on a
  finding at step 8 that requires a code change? Step 8 says rerun tests and the
  verifier and "obtain fresh review approval". Who grants it? Is that loop
  bounded, and does it agree with step 7's "not the whole battery again"?
- Step 8 says '/code-review' "exists only where someone has installed it
  themselves - check before relying on it". So what is the mandated review
  mechanism when it is absent? Are the PreToolUse hooks sufficient given they
  only fire on 'git push' and 'gh pr create' - i.e. AFTER the commit that step 8
  is supposed to gate? Read the hook prompts in .claude/settings.json and note
  what they actually review and when.
- Step 2 ("create a branch first") versus step 1 and versus the verifier's own
  note that 'git diff main...HEAD' is routinely empty. Any contradiction?
- Steps 10-12: PR and merge. Step 12 requires "every configured check passes" -
  does this repository configure any CI check? Look for .github/workflows.
  If none exists, say what step 12 actually reduces to.
- Step 11 says "re-run steps 6 to 9 for whatever changed" - is that consistent
  with step 10's "Rerun code review only if the reviewed state changed"?
- Anything a reader would reasonably do that the steps never authorise, or
  conversely any instruction with no stopping condition.

Report only defects you can evidence.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'split-and-mutation',
    prompt: `${CONTEXT}

LENS: step 7's main-agent/verifier split table and the mutation-testing regime.

Check specifically:
- Every row of the table against docs/VERIFIER.md. Is each check the table
  assigns to the verifier actually commanded in docs/VERIFIER.md's own
  instructions (the part from '## The checks' down), and vice versa? Name any
  check that appears in the table but is only DESCRIBED, not COMMANDED, in the
  doc - or the reverse.
- The main-agent column lists "The whole unit project once a slice is done" and
  "npm run lint, npx tsc --noEmit"; the verifier column lists the same three
  again. AGENTS.md calls this a deliberate exception. Is the rationale sound and
  is it stated in both files, or only one?
- The mutation regime: the main agent runs mutants and must "name each mutant
  and the suite that caught it when invoking the verifier". Is there any
  mechanism that fails when it doesn't? docs/VERIFIER.md says "Silence is also a
  finding" - but the verifier cannot distinguish "no mutants warranted" from
  "mutants run and not reported". Is that gap acknowledged and is the guidance
  actionable?
- "Choose mutants to defeat the assertion, not to confirm it" - is that
  instruction operational enough to follow, or is it only a narrative of #248?
  Is there a checklist an agent could actually execute?
- Playwright: the table gives the main agent "The single Playwright spec whose
  journey changed" and the verifier the full run. But AGENTS.md's Gotchas say a
  Playwright run fails in global-teardown if it leaves data behind, and that a
  partial/interrupted run trips it. Does running ONE spec then the FULL suite
  interact badly? Read playwright.config.ts, e2e/global-setup and
  global-teardown if present.
- Does anything own the security-sensitive checks - migrations with
  RAISE EXCEPTION guards, the sanitize-standalone step, DATABASE_IS_DISPOSABLE?

Report only defects you can evidence.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'guard-rigor',
    prompt: `${CONTEXT}

LENS: does __tests__/docs/agentInstructions.test.ts actually pin what it claims?

Apply the repository's OWN standard from AGENTS.md step 7: "Choose mutants to
defeat the assertion, not to confirm it. Ask what edit would leave this test
green while making it meaningless." Do that to this test file, on paper - DO NOT
EDIT ANY FILE, do not run anything that writes to the tree. Reason from the
source. You may run 'npm run test:unit -- --testPathPattern agentInstructions'
read-only to see the current state, but change nothing.

For each assertion in the file, name the edit to AGENTS.md, docs/VERIFIER.md,
docs/UI_REVIEW.md or .claude/agents/*.md that would gut the guarantee while
leaving the test green. Specifically interrogate:
- CHECKS_THE_VERIFIER_OWNS: the patterns are bare tokens like /mutant/,
  /selection/, /populated/, /database project/. What wording change satisfies the
  regex while removing the obligation? The file's own comment admits rewording
  passes - is the admission enough, or should the guard be stronger?
- The 'gives %s no tool its instructions say it does not have' test. It bars
  Edit/Write/Task by name. ui-review holds Bash and
  mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_evaluate. Does the test's premise -
  that the tools line reflects the doc's claims - hold for ui-review? Would
  granting a NEW writing-capable tool (a plugin MCP tool, browser_run_code_unsafe)
  be caught?
- expect(...instructions).toMatch(/you have no|cannot delegate/i) - how
  load-bearing is that, given docs/UI_REVIEW.md says "you have no editing tools"
  which is false while it holds Bash?
- The 'points at instructions that exist and say something' test uses
  >20 lines. What passes it while being useless?
- What is NOT guarded at all: docs/UI_REVIEW.md content, the ui-review side of
  the split, whether AGENTS.md steps 1-12 still exist, whether the hooks in
  .claude/settings.json still match what step 8 describes.

Report only defects you can evidence, each with the concrete gutting edit.`,
  },
]

phase('Analyze')

const perDimension = await pipeline(
  DIMENSIONS,
  d => agent(d.prompt, { label: `analyze:${d.key}`, phase: 'Analyze', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA }),
  (result, d) => {
    if (!result || !result.findings || result.findings.length === 0) return []
    // Cap adversarial verification at the two most severe per lens.
    const order = { blocking: 0, high: 1, medium: 2, low: 3 }
    const ranked = [...result.findings].sort(
      (a, b) => (order[a.severity] ?? 9) - (order[b.severity] ?? 9),
    )
    const top = ranked.slice(0, 2)
    const rest = ranked.slice(2).map(f => ({ ...f, lens: d.key, verdict: null }))
    if (ranked.length > 2) {
      log(`${d.key}: ${ranked.length} findings, adversarially verifying the top 2`)
    }
    return parallel(
      top.map(f => () =>
        agent(
          `${CONTEXT}

You are an adversarial verifier. Your job is to REFUTE the following claim about
this repository's agent workflow. Default to refuted=true unless the evidence on
disk plainly supports it.

CLAIM: ${f.title}
LOCATION: ${f.location}
EVIDENCE OFFERED: ${f.evidence}
CLAIMED IMPACT: ${f.impact}
PROPOSED FIX: ${f.proposed_fix}

Read the actual files. Refute it if: the quoted text does not say what is
claimed, the concern is already handled elsewhere in AGENTS.md or docs/, the
claim rests on a misunderstanding of how Claude Code resolves sub-agents or
tools, it is a style preference rather than a defect, or the proposed fix would
not actually fix it. Change nothing on disk.

If the finding is real but the details or the fix are wrong, set refuted=false
and give the corrected claim and corrected fix.`,
          { label: `refute:${d.key}`, phase: 'Refute', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA },
        ).then(v => ({ ...f, lens: d.key, verdict: v })),
      ),
    ).then(verified => [...verified.filter(Boolean), ...rest])
  },
)

const all = perDimension.flat().filter(Boolean)
const survivors = all.filter(f => !f.verdict || f.verdict.refuted !== true)
const refuted = all.filter(f => f.verdict && f.verdict.refuted === true)

log(`${all.length} findings raised, ${refuted.length} refuted, ${survivors.length} standing`)

phase('Synthesize')

const synthesis = await agent(
  `${CONTEXT}

You are synthesising a review of this repository's agent workflow. Below are the
findings that survived adversarial verification, plus the ones that were
refuted (listed so you do not resurrect them).

SURVIVING FINDINGS:
${JSON.stringify(survivors, null, 2)}

REFUTED (do not resurrect):
${JSON.stringify(refuted.map(f => ({ title: f.title, why_refuted: f.verdict.reason })), null, 2)}

Read AGENTS.md, docs/VERIFIER.md, docs/UI_REVIEW.md, .claude/agents/*.md and
__tests__/docs/agentInstructions.test.ts yourself before writing anything -
the findings may overlap, contradict, or propose fixes that collide.

Produce:
1. A deduplicated, severity-ranked list of the real problems. Where a verifier
   supplied a corrected_claim or corrected_fix, use the corrected version.
2. For each, the CONCRETE edit: which file, which passage, what the replacement
   text should be. Be specific enough that someone could apply it without
   re-deriving the analysis. Where the fix is to AGENTS.md prose, draft the
   actual replacement sentences in the repository's existing voice - terse,
   evidence-first, citing issue numbers where the existing text does.
3. Explicitly flag any proposed edit that would break
   __tests__/docs/agentInstructions.test.ts, and say what the test needs to
   become.
4. A short "no change needed" section for things that look wrong but are
   deliberate, so the reader is not tempted to re-open them.

Keep it tight. This is a proposal a human will read and decide on, not a report
about a report. Return markdown.`,
  { label: 'synthesize', phase: 'Synthesize' },
)

return { synthesis, survivorCount: survivors.length, refutedCount: refuted.length }

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.
