Mona AirwaysAGENTS.md · docs/ · .claude/agents/13 agents · 749k tokens

The workflow is well-reasoned and under-enforced

Four independent lenses over the twelve-step workflow, the two sub-agent definitions and the guard test that pins them, each finding run past an adversarial verifier. The rules are sound. What is missing is the machinery that makes them true — and the guard test protecting them is green against edits that would gut it.

Raised
37
Refuted
4
Standing
29
Sub-agents correct
1 of 2

Tier 1 — the rulebook makes an agent do the wrong thing

Each of these is a documented rule that does not hold, or an obligation with no way to discharge it. All seven were spot-checked against the files on disk.

01HighAGENTS.md:39–41 · jest.database-setup.js

AGENTS.md says the database Jest project refuses to run against a non-disposable database. It does not.

The claim is that “a Playwright run and the database Jest project delete every booking in the database they are pointed at, and refuse to start without it.” The project's globalSetup is jest.database-setup.js, whose only export is assertSerialised — it throws on maxWorkers > 1 and checks nothing else. Verified: the string DATABASE_IS_DISPOSABLE appears in exactly one source file, e2e/global-setup.ts:99.

The real check, assertDisposableDatabase(), is reached from the Jest project only through clearPreviousRunBookings, imported by a single test (__tests__/e2e/runIsolation.database.test.ts:71) — lazily, in Jest's file order, after the other database test files have already written and deleted.

Fix — code, so the doc becomes true

Extract the destination check to CommonJS (scripts/assertDisposableDatabase.js), import it from e2e/global-setup.ts, and call it in jest.database-setup.js beside assertSerialised. Do not require() the .ts file from a globalSetup — transform coverage there is version-dependent, and this must fail closed rather than fail to load. If the code fix is deferred, AGENTS.md must instead say plainly that the Jest project deletes rows but does not refuse.

02Highdocs/UI_REVIEW.md:10

ui-review is told it has no editing tools. It has Bash, and no rule in place of the false claim.

“You do not fix: you have no editing tools, and that is deliberate.” The definition grants Bash (.claude/agents/ui-review.md:4) and the doc itself orders its use (npm run dev, line 39). docs/VERIFIER.md:13–17 states the honest version for the sibling agent — “sed -i is not a loophole: change nothing git status would report” — and nothing equivalent exists here. ui-review runs immediately before the verifier certifies the tree.

browser_evaluate is not part of this. It mutates an ephemeral DOM and a database the review is supposed to drive. The hazard is tracked source via Bash.

Fix

Replace lines 10–11 with the verifier's formulation, scoped the same way: the rule is “change nothing git status would report”; a dev server, .next/, screenshots and data created by driving the app are explicitly not violations. Keep the phrase “you have no” until finding 08 lands — the guard test currently matches on it.

03Highdocs/VERIFIER.md:60 · package.json:13

The verifier's sole instruction for its solely-owned database project is npm test, which short-circuits.

"test": "npm run test:unit && npm run test:database". AGENTS.md says so outright at line 74. docs/VERIFIER.md:60 is the only Jest command anywhere in docs/, and it is what backs the verifier's ownership of “the full unit and database projects”.

The exposure is the path the workflow explicitly anticipates: a unit failure classified pre-existing and resolved without a code change. There is then no rerun, the database project never runs against the final tree, and “an unrun check is not a passing one” (line 167) is silently unsatisfiable — the verifier does not know it was unrun. The file already documents the two neighbouring traps in these same scripts; this is the missing third.

Fix

Split line 60 into npm run test:unit and npm run test:database as separate commands, reported separately, never chained. Add the trap to Environment traps that produce false results, beside its two siblings. Keep the literal “database project” — the guard test matches it.

04HighAGENTS.md:228–231

Step 7 requires a main baseline that no step produces, and the cost split forbids measuring it.

“Say what is failing on main when invoking it, or the classification is a guess dressed as a result.” Every mention of the baseline consumes one; nothing produces one. Steps 1 and 2 are the only moments the agent stands on main, and neither says anything. Meanwhile the split assigns the build, the full Playwright run and the database project to the verifier and forbids duplicating them — so for three of the five columns a baseline is unobtainable by design.

Fix — append to step 2
While still on main, run npm run lint and npm run test:unit 2>&1 | grep -E '^Tests:' and keep the result — that record is the baseline step 7 requires you to hand the verifier. You do not own the build, the database project or the full Playwright run, so you will have no baseline for those: say so in the invocation rather than leaving it unstated. An invented baseline is worse than a missing one, because a real regression gets waved through as pre-existing on your say-so.
05HighAGENTS.md:190–191

The “mutant table” both documents audit is never defined as a deliverable.

AGENTS.md requires only “name each mutant and the suite that caught it.” But AGENTS.md:217–221 and docs/VERIFIER.md:133–136 reason about a table, per-mutant outcomes, and whether each died on the first attempt — none of which that requirement produces. The verifier is also told to “read the test it named” and to judge whether an assertion constrains the mutated value, while AGENTS.md supplies a suite and no edit.

Fix

Make the deliverable explicit: hand the verifier a mutant table, one row per mutant — file:line, the exact edit, the suite run, died or survived, and whether it died on the first attempt. Change docs/VERIFIER.md:128 from “the test it named” to “the test the row names”. Land this before finding 11, which pins the new wording.

06HighAGENTS.md:281–283

Step 8's review → verifier loop is unbounded and self-perpetuating.

Step 8 names no inputs to the re-run, while step 7 makes two compulsory (the mutant table, the main baseline). docs/VERIFIER.md:153–157 guarantees that an invocation with no mutant named produces a coverage finding; step 7 makes that actionable; step 8 then mandates another verifier run — which can again arrive without the table. Every neighbouring loop in these documents is capped. This one is not, and it collides with “prefer one thorough pass to several narrow ones.”

Fix

Batch the findings, rerun the verifier once per review round carrying forward the same baseline and mutant table, and make the exit explicit: “If a second round still requires code changes, the slice is too large: stop and split it per step 3 rather than looping.”

07High.claude/agents/ui-review.md:4

ui-review's core tools come from an optional plugin. No file says so, and none names a fallback.

All seventeen browser tools are prefixed mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__. There is no .mcp.json and .claude/settings.json declares no plugins — so on a machine without that plugin the allowlist resolves to Read/Grep/Glob/Bash and step 6 is unperformable, while docs/UI_REVIEW.md:36–38 forbids the degraded substitute and AGENTS.md then requires the main agent to address an unaddressable finding.

The contrast is self-inflicted: AGENTS.md gives precisely this warning for /code-review, which is the optional dependency.

Fix

Say in step 6 that the rendered pass depends on an installed plugin — check before relying on it, as with /code-review in step 8. Where absent, ui-review announces it at the top of its report and drives the journey through a scratch Playwright script written outside the repository (@playwright/test is already a devDependency, and a file outside the tree does not violate finding 02's rule). Recording “no browser tooling” as a completed UI review is not acceptable. Mirror it in docs/UI_REVIEW.md.

Tier 2 — guards that are green while pinning nothing

The repository's own standard, applied to the file that enforces it: what edit would leave this test green while making it meaningless? Each edit below was traced on paper against __tests__/docs/agentInstructions.test.ts; nothing was written to the tree. Apply the prescribed mutant — delete the section, do not reword it — when fixing each.

08HighagentInstructions.test.ts:287

toMatch(/you have no|cannot delegate/i) certifies a false claim and survives deletion of the rule it protects.

Two independent defects in one assertion. For docs/UI_REVIEW.md, the only matching text is the false sentence in finding 02 — the comment promises the check protects toolset claims; it protects the existence of a phrase. For docs/VERIFIER.md, deleting lines 13–17 wholesale — the entire “change nothing git status would report” paragraph — leaves the regex satisfied by line 108 (“You cannot delegate — you have no Task tool”), which is about a run-count cap. Suite stays green.

Fix

Replace the phrase-match with a per-file rule list, matched against whitespace-normalised text (docs/VERIFIER.md hard-wraps “no Task\ntool”, so a naive /no Task tool/ does not match and a reflow would read as a deleted rule). Then tie the claim to the grant rather than a fixed phrase:

if (granted.includes('Bash')) expect(stated).toMatch(/Bash can write/);

That is the assertion that would have caught docs/UI_REVIEW.md:10.

09HighagentInstructions.test.ts:76

TOOLS_THE_INSTRUCTIONS_RULE_OUT is a three-name denylist.

It bars Edit, Write, Task. Appending NotebookEdit to the verifier, or browser_run_code_unsafe to ui-review — a real tool on the same plugin server as the seventeen already granted — passes all 21 tests.

Fix

Invert to a per-definition allowlist and assert set equality. Keep expect(granted).toContain('Read') as the arming check, and keep the denylist loop for its clearer failure message.

10HighagentInstructions.test.ts:113,117

/mutant/ and /selection/ match incidental prose, so both audit obligations are deletable.

Matched against everything from ## The checks down, where “mutant” occurs eight times and “selection” twice. Deleting the paragraph that assigns the claim audit, or the one that assigns the selection audit, leaves both green — /selection/ is satisfied by the line telling the verifier not to report a missing survivor.

Fix — and a warning

Point each pattern at the assigning sentence: /audit of every mutant/ against the table cell, /audit the claim rather than taking it/ against the prose; /and of the selection/ and /Audit the \*selection\* as well as each claim/. This requires widening the tuple to three elements, because the same pattern is currently asserted against both sides and the assigning sentences differ. A single-pattern version turns the suite red on a correct tree.

11HighagentInstructions.test.ts:135–176

Everything in step 7 except the table is unguarded.

checksAssignedToTheVerifier reads the anchor and column 2 of the table, nothing else. Deleting AGENTS.md:185–231 in one block removes the whole mutation discipline (#248), the mutant-reporting requirement (#231) and the main baseline rule — 21 of 21 green.

Fix

Add a STEP_SEVEN_OBLIGATIONS array asserted against the step 7 body, sliced between the step 7 and step 8 headings: the mutant table, the selection rule, the main baseline, the settled-tree rule. Land findings 05 and 04 first — the patterns pin their new wording.

12HighagentInstructions.test.ts:248–249

docs/UI_REVIEW.md is guarded by a line count and one loose regex.

The only assertions reaching the file are “more than 20 lines” and the phrase-match in finding 08. Replacing all 77 lines with 21 lines of “Skim the diff. If it looks fine, say so and stop.” passes. The line count is separately worthless — trim() strips only the ends, so 'x' + '\n'.repeat(20) + 'y' scores 21. This is the line-limit defect from #248, reintroduced inside the test that documents it.

Fix

Add CHECKS_THE_UI_REVIEWER_OWNS asserted per side, as step 7 already is — three viewports, visual evidence, an explicit not-applicable. Replace the line count with the one thing a real instruction file has and a placeholder does not: the read-from-disk clause present in both docs.

13MediumagentInstructions.test.ts:46–49 · AGENTS.md:234

.claude/agents/ is never enumerated, and AGENTS.md states a universal that entire-search.md breaks.

The pointer list is hard-coded. Adding .claude/agents/reviewer.md with an inline body and no tools: line — which by the test's own error text means it inherits every tool — passes all 21. Separately, “The definitions under .claude/agents/ are pointers at them and carry no rules” is false of entire-search.md, eighteen lines of rules. The exemption exists only inside a JSDoc comment in a test, so an agent following AGENTS.md converts a generated file into a pointer and the generator overwrites it.

Fix

Enumerate the directory and partition on the ENTIRE-MANAGED marker, asserting the exempt set is exactly ['entire-search.md'] so a vanished marker goes red. Attack it by adding a fixture definition, not by editing an existing one. In AGENTS.md, name the two definitions this repository authors and state the entire-search.md exemption in the prose.

14MediumagentInstructions.test.ts:218–233

The AGENTS.md guard checks that eight ## headings exist. Whole workflow steps can be deleted.

Deleting step 6 and step 8 leaves 21 of 21 green — and .claude/agents/ui-review.md stays perfectly configured while nothing requires it to be invoked.

Fix

Slice ## Development Workflow → ## Testing Expectations and assert all twelve numbered items by their bolded title. Fails on deletion or renumbering; tolerates body edits.

15Medium.claude/settings.json:37–51

Nothing checks that the hooks step 8 leans on still exist.

Step 8 asserts the PreToolUse hooks “run without being asked” and rests the whole review model on them; /code-review is already documented as absent here, so those two hooks are the entire automated pre-commit review. grep -rn "settings.json" __tests__/ returns nothing. Deleting both "type": "agent" entries passes everything.

Fix

Parse .claude/settings.json and assert both hooks exist with their if: filters and their FAIL clause, and that both command strings appear in AGENTS.md step 8 so config and doc cannot drift apart.

Tier 3 — real but narrower

Findings 16–24 in the working set, condensed. Each still carries a concrete edit.

16Mediumdocs/UI_REVIEW.md:46,70

ui-review's screenshots never reach the caller.

“Capture a screenshot at each” and “Reference the screenshots you took” name no path. A sub-agent returns text, so the images are discarded on return — while step 6 makes them a workflow requirement the main agent must reason from, including when justifying the dismissal of a finding about rendering it never sees. Write them under test-results/ui-review/ (already gitignored) and list the paths in the report. Add /.playwright-mcp/ to .gitignore, the MCP default output directory, so finding 02's rule needs no screenshot carve-out.

17Mediumdocs/UI_REVIEW.md:25–30

ui-review leads with the diff range its sibling warns is routinely empty — then authorises stopping on it.

docs/VERIFIER.md:36–38 warns its agent plainly that git diff main...HEAD is empty pre-commit. docs/UI_REVIEW.md gives the same instruction with the warning removed and the order reversed, then grants an exit phrased over “the diff” — making “the diff is empty, therefore nothing can alter rendered output” a locally valid read that step 6 accepts as a complete result. Reorder to put uncommitted files first and carry the warning across.

18MediumAGENTS.md:155–157

“rerun the verifier — not the whole battery again” is ambiguous, and one reading is countermanded.

The clause can attach to either agent. Under the reading where the verifier narrows its run, docs/VERIFIER.md:42–48 flatly refuses — “cost is never a reason to skip one… If you skip one of those, nothing else runs it” — and there is no mechanism by which the caller could scope a verifier run anyway. Rewrite so the reduction plainly belongs to the main agent.

19MediumAGENTS.md:238–240

“Say so in the invocation” is inert for a toolset change.

It works for a changed pointer. It cannot work for a changed tools: line: the allowlist is bound when the session registers the definition, and no message grants or revokes a tool afterwards. Say instead that a toolset change takes effect on the next session, and do not try to verify one in the session that made it.

20MediumAGENTS.md:195–214

The executable mutant taxonomy lives only in the auditor's file.

The agent choosing mutants gets one question and four anecdotes; the agent auditing them gets the generalised checklist in docs/VERIFIER.md:136–139 — and nothing tells the main agent to read that file. Move the list up: a bound with headroom, a superset/subset matcher, a literal string search, a guard over a document or table, an assertion after an early return. Then cut the four-anecdote block to a one-line pointer at #248, keeping the “everything died is more ambiguous, not stronger” passage intact.

21Mediumdocs/VERIFIER.md:153–157

“Silence is also a finding” has no trigger on the main agent's side.

The verifier is told the main agent “is required to name them”, but mutation testing appears nowhere in AGENTS.md outside step 7, whose strongest statement is about ownership and scope rather than when. Testing Expectations never mentions it; step 4's TDD loop has no mutation step. Add the trigger to Testing Expectations, and let the verifier stand down when the invocation says why none was warranted.

22Mediume2e/global-setup.ts:193

The main agent's single-spec Playwright runs launder their leaks into the verifier's baseline.

Every run records the database as it found it, and leak detection reports only ids absent from that snapshot. A failed spec whose afterAll never finished leaves rows that are present when the verifier snapshots — so they are never reported (#213), and leaked Flight/FlightSchedule rows are not inert (#173). Add a bullet to step 7: re-run that spec green, or delete its rows, before invoking the verifier.

23Medium.agents/agents/verify/agent.json:10

A second, fully inline verifier definition lives outside the guarded set.

It carries the whole role in systemPromptSections[0].content — the pattern step 7 forbids — with five verification steps containing no migration run, no mutation audit and no flake protocol, and it grants run_command with no “change nothing” rule. It is unreachable from AGENT_DEFINITION_POINTERS. Verified present on disk.

Recommendation — delete .agents/agents/verify/

Nothing in the repository consumes it. Flagged test impact: __tests__/security/committedSecrets.test.ts:57 uses that exact path as its arming assertion — re-point it at AGENTS.md in the same commit, and tidy the .agents entry in containerSecrets.test.ts:19. If the harness is still in use, the alternative is to convert it to the same pointer body and add it to the guarded set with a JSON-aware extractor.

24MediumAGENTS.md:295–319 · .github/workflows/ci.yml

Steps 10–12 never tell the agent to observe CI, though step 12 gates on it.

CI runs on every pull request against main and spans lint, typecheck, npm test, Playwright and two Docker builds — minutes. Step 10 ends at “push and create the pull request”; step 11 is conditional on findings arriving; gh pr checks appears nowhere and is not in permissions.allow. The path from PR created to merge has no observation point, so a clean-but-pending state reads as clean — the bypass step 12 forbids. Add gh pr checks <n> --watch to step 10, and allow Bash(gh pr checks:*) and Bash(gh pr view:*).

Tier 4 — low, plus two the fan-out missed

Findings 27 and 28 came from checking CI and package.json directly rather than from the four lenses.

25LowAGENTS.md:308–312

Step 11 re-runs steps 6–9 for any finding, with no proportionality.

Steps 6 and 7 are sub-agent invocations whose scope the sub-agent decides from the diff, so “for whatever changed” is undefined there — and step 7 grants itself a reduction that step 11 does not inherit. A comment-typo fix triggers a full rendered pass and a full battery. Scope it by reach: step 6 if rendered output changes, step 7 if behaviour or the build changes, step 8 always.

26LowAGENTS.md:257–261

“Ask a sub-agent whether it is real” names no sub-agent, and the nearest match is the wrong one.

The closest description is the verifier's, which is scoped to the full battery and would spend minutes on a one-line question. Neither general-purpose nor Explore is named anywhere in AGENTS.md. Name general-purpose explicitly in both places, and optionally narrow the verifier's frontmatter description to “runs the full build/test battery for a finished change” so the registry routes correctly. Editing frontmatter does not break the pointer test — bodyOf slices past it.

27Low.claude/agents/*.md:5

model: and name: are unconstrained by the guard.

bodyOf starts after the frontmatter and the tools check reads only /^tools:(.*)$/m, so changing model: inherit to model: haiku passes all 21 — silently downgrading the agent that audits mutation claims from source. Assert ^model: inherit$ and that name: matches the filename.

28Medium.github/workflows/ci.yml:36 · AGENTS.md “Commands”

Two CI-only gates are documented nowhere, so an agent meets them for the first time on a red pull request.

CI runs npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high and a container secret scan with two negative probes (scripts/verify-container-secrets.sh, a layer-sentinel build and an env-file build, each of which must be rejected). AGENTS.md mentions only that “CI asserts no secret survives in any image layer” and never names the audit step or the file. A dependency bump that trips the audit, or a Dockerfile change that breaks a probe, is invisible until after the push. List both under Commands with the caveat that the verifier does not own them.

29Lowpackage.json:16–17

inventory:generate and inventory:check are owned by nobody.

scripts/generate-inventory.ts and scripts/check-inventory.ts exist and are referenced in no other file — not AGENTS.md, not docs/, not CI. Either wire inventory:check into the verifier's column and CI, or delete the pair. A script that nothing runs and nothing documents is drift with a maintenance cost.

Test impact

Where a proposed edit collides with __tests__/docs/agentInstructions.test.ts or its neighbours.

EditEffect
02 — UI_REVIEW:10Safe only while the replacement keeps “you have no”. Land 08 first to drop the phrase.
03 — VERIFIER:60/database project/ is load-bearing. The replacement comment must keep that literal.
05 — mutant tableSafe today; 11's new pattern pins the new wording. Land 05 before 11.
10 — audit patternsRequires changing the tuple arity of CHECKS_THE_VERIFIER_OWNS and both assertions. Single-pattern versions go red on a correct tree.
12 — UI_REVIEW guardDeletes the “> 20 lines” assertion rather than keeping it.
13 — enumerate agentsReplaces the hard-coded pointer list; it.each still consumes the same shape.
23 — delete .agents/Breaks committedSecrets.test.ts:57. Re-point the arming assertion in the same commit.
Any AGENTS.md editMust preserve the **The verifier owns the slow checks anchor, the table, and the exact header | Main agent | Verifier |. Three tests throw with a different message if these move.

Settled — deliberate, do not re-open

Four claims were raised and refuted. Recorded here so they are not rediscovered.

  • Port 3000 and ui-review leaving a dev server. Already assigned to whoever runs Playwright, and both sub-agents are sent to AGENTS.md. A teardown clause would be a no-op in the common case, where the server is the developer's own.
  • The verifier's tree rule is not over-broad. It already scopes itself: build output, a generated Prisma client, scratch databases and untracked files outside the repository are fine. “The line is tracked source.”
  • Step 8 has a performer and a grantor — the main agent. The workflow is a first-person procedure; steps 1–5 and 9–12 name no grantor either. “Neither is a bespoke sub-agent” is the instruction that this pass is not delegated.
  • Steps 1 and 5 do not contradict. Step 5 removes changes while preserving work that belongs to the user; step 1 preserves pre-existing work. Both point the same way.
  • entire-search.md carrying inline rules is correct. It is generated and marked ENTIRE-MANAGED. Finding 13 makes the exemption explicit and asserted rather than removing it.
  • “Do not report the absence of a survivor as a finding” is deliberate. A survivor is a diagnostic, not a quota. Do not add a survivor requirement to finding 05's table schema.
  • /code-review being absent here is documented, not a defect. Finding 07 asks step 6 to get the same treatment — not for the plugin to be installed.

# AGENTS

Next.js 16 App Router + Prisma/PostgreSQL + NextAuth. TypeScript strict, Tailwind, shadcn/ui.

These instructions govern all feature, fix, refactor, documentation, and
maintenance work in this repository. All agents and sub-agents must follow them.

This is the only file that carries agent rules. The sub-agents' instructions are
in [Sub-agents](#sub-agents) below rather than in their own documents, because
two files describing one split drift: a check named in one and reworded in the
other is owned by nobody, and five such gaps reached a review at once. The
definitions under `.claude/agents/` point here and carry no rules of their own —
see [Sub-agents](#sub-agents) for why.

## Commands

```bash
npm ci                      # Node 22 required (.npmrc engine-strict blocks other majors)
npm run dev                 # http://localhost:3000
npm run lint                # eslint app components lib
npx tsc --noEmit            # typecheck (no npm script)
npm test                    # Jest, both projects — needs a running Postgres (see Gotchas)
npm run test:unit -- --testPathPattern flightTime   # one file; see Gotchas before using a bare path
npm run test:database       # the *.database.test.ts project, serialised
npx playwright test         # E2E; starts its own dev server, so free port 3000 first
npm run build               # next build + scripts/sanitize-standalone.mjs
```

```bash
docker compose up --build         # full stack: db + mailpit + proxy, migrates and seeds
docker compose up -d db mailpit   # just the services Jest and Playwright need
npx prisma migrate deploy && npx prisma db seed
```

Two gates run only in CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) and nothing local covers
them, so a change that trips one is invisible until the pull request goes red:

```bash
npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high        # blocks on a high-severity production advisory
./scripts/verify-container-secrets.sh <image>  # plus two probe builds CI expects to be REJECTED
```

Run the audit yourself after any dependency change. The container scan needs a
built image and belongs to whoever touches the `Dockerfile`, the standalone
output or `scripts/sanitize-standalone.mjs`.

## Environment

`cp .env.example .env`, then generate three secrets:

- `NEXTAUTH_SECRET` — 32+ characters
- `PASSENGER_DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEYS` — `local-v1:$(openssl rand -base64 32)`
- `STAFF_MFA_ENCRYPTION_KEYS` — a *different* `local-v1:$(openssl rand -base64 32)`

`lib/env.ts` validates all eight required variables fail-closed at boot (via
`instrumentation.ts`). A malformed key ring crashes startup rather than degrading.

`.env.example` also carries `DATABASE_IS_DISPOSABLE=true`. A Playwright run and the
database Jest project delete every booking in the database they are pointed at, and
refuse to start without it — host and name cannot tell a developer's database from a
deployment, since Compose gives the application the same pair. Never set it where
this application is deployed.

Local verification and recovery email lands in Mailpit at http://localhost:8025.

Never commit a secret value or pass one on the command line. Every environment
that runs this application injects configuration at runtime.

## Architecture

- `app/actions.ts` — `'use server'`; the primary mutation path for the whole app
- `app/api/` — auth routes only (register, verify, password reset, NextAuth)
- `lib/*Service.ts` — data and business logic, called from server actions
- `lib/validation.ts` — shared Zod schemas; mutations parse through `parseActionInput`
- `lib/actionResult.ts` — mutations return `{ ok: false, error }` instead of throwing on validation failure
- `prisma/schema.prisma` — migrations are hand-authored SQL, several security-critical

## Gotchas

- A migration that fails leaves Prisma refusing to apply anything else: the next
  `migrate deploy` reports `P3009`, not the original error. Fix the data the migration
  objected to, then `npx prisma migrate resolve --rolled-back <migration_name>` before
  deploying again. A failed migration rolls back whole — no half-created type or
  column survives — so the retry is clean. Several migrations here `RAISE EXCEPTION`
  deliberately rather than let a cast fail with a less useful message, so this is a
  normal path rather than a disaster
- There are no down migrations. Rolling one back means reversing its SQL by hand and
  deleting its row from `_prisma_migrations`; write the reversal in the migration's
  header comment when it is not obvious
- `__tests__/**/*.database.test.ts` require a live Postgres; start it before `npm test`
- Those files run serially in their own Jest project: they share one database and
  several assert against whole tables, so running them beside each other counted one
  file's fixtures in another file's scan (#155). `npm test` runs the unit project
  first and stops if it fails, so pass flags to `test:unit`/`test:database` directly
  rather than to `npm test`, which does not forward them. What serialises them is
  `--runInBand` in the `test:database` script, not the config, so the project's
  `globalSetup` refuses any run it is not given — `npx jest --selectProjects
  database` stops with a message naming the worker count rather than
  reproducing the interference the split removed (#215)
- `npm test` is `test:unit && test:database`. A failing unit test means the database
  project never ran at all — not that it passed. Run it separately before concluding
  anything about it
- `npm run test:unit -- <path>` does **not** filter: it runs all of them and says nothing.
  The script ends in `--selectProjects unit`, which takes a list, so the path is read as
  another project name and ignored. Filter with `-- --testPathPattern <regex>` or
  `-- -t '<test name>'`. `npm run test:database -- <path>` does filter, because
  `--runInBand` sits between the project list and the path — which is exactly why the
  difference is easy to miss
- Node-environment tests need `/** @jest-environment node */` (jsdom is the Jest default)
- Playwright runs `workers: 1, fullyParallel: false` on purpose — parallel runs collide on the DB
- A Playwright run fails in `global-teardown` if it left accounts, tokens, reviews,
  favorites, notifications, flights or schedules behind. `global-setup` cannot delete
  those — it cannot tell a run's account from a developer's — so each spec deletes what
  it created in a `test.afterAll`, and the teardown compares snapshots to catch the ones
  that do not (#213). Two things trip it that are not a leak: a failing or interrupted
  test, whose `afterAll` never finished, and anything else writing to the same database
  during the run. Fix the failure, or run the suite alone, rather than the report
- Always `npm run build`, never bare `next build`: the sanitize step strips `.env` files from
  standalone output, and CI asserts no secret survives in any image layer
- Staff mutations gate on `hasVerifiedStaffAccess(session)` — a session alone is not enough;
  staff must complete TOTP enrollment (`docs/STAFF_ACCOUNT_POLICY.md`)

## Code Style

4-space indent, single quotes, semicolons. The `@/*` path alias maps to the repo root.
Chart and other browser-interactive components need `'use client'`.

## Development Workflow

1. **Inspect before changing anything.** Inspect the repository, current Git
   state, and all applicable instruction files before making changes. Preserve
   unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked work.

2. **Create a branch first.** Create a dedicated feature, fix, refactor, chore,
   test, or documentation branch before making code changes. Never commit
   directly to `main`, and create the branch from the latest appropriate
   `main` state.

   While still on `main`, run `npm run lint` and
   `npm run test:unit 2>&1 | grep -E '^Tests:'` and keep the result. That record
   is the baseline step 7 requires you to hand the verifier, and this is the only
   moment you are standing on `main` to take it. You do not own the build, the
   database project or the full Playwright run, so you will have no baseline for
   those — say so when you invoke the verifier rather than leaving it unstated.
   An invented baseline is worse than a missing one, because a real regression
   gets waved through as pre-existing on your say-so.

3. **Choose a thin vertical slice.** Before implementing a tracked issue or
   feature, define the smallest end-to-end slice that can be reviewed, tested,
   shipped, and merged independently. Prefer one coherent user-visible or
   operational outcome over a broad horizontal layer. If the next issue is too
   large for one pull request, split it into ordered slices and complete only
   the current slice. Keep pull requests small enough for thorough review,
   reliable verification, and quick rollback. When work surfaces a defect or
   improvement that belongs outside the current slice, do not widen the slice
   to absorb it — file it as described under Issue Tracking and carry on.

4. **Use test-driven development when behavior or structure is testable.**
   - Add or update a focused test before implementation.
   - Run it and confirm it fails for the expected reason.
   - Implement the smallest appropriate change.
   - Run focused tests while iterating.
   - Refactor only while the relevant tests remain green.

5. **Inspect the complete diff.** Review the branch diff plus all staged,
   unstaged, and untracked files. Remove accidental or unrelated changes while
   preserving work that belongs to the user.

6. **Run `ui-review` before verification.** After the main agent completes an
   implementation pass, invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent, whose instructions are
   under [Sub-agents](#ui-review). Address every actionable finding before
   running the `verifier`. For changes with no UI impact, explicitly record that
   rendered UI review is not applicable. If a finding is not applicable, record
   the concrete reason rather than silently ignoring it.

   The rendered pass depends on the `mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_*`
   tools listed on `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`. Those come from an installed
   plugin rather than from this repository — check they are present before
   relying on them, as with `/code-review` in step 8. Where they are absent the
   sub-agent falls back to a throwaway Playwright script and says so at the top
   of its report; "no browser tooling" recorded as a completed UI review is not
   acceptable.

7. **Run `verifier` before code review.** Invoke the `verifier` sub-agent, whose
   instructions are under [Sub-agents](#verifier). It runs the builds, static
   checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for the change, and reports
   failures, flakes, missing coverage, and environment issues. Fix or explicitly
   resolve every actionable finding before starting code review. If a finding
   requires a code change, rerun the focused tests for that change yourself and
   then hand the settled tree back — do not re-run the whole battery yourself
   first, because the verifier always runs its own column and you cannot scope
   its run.

   **The verifier owns the slow checks; do not run them twice.** Split it by
   what a check costs:

   | Main agent | Verifier |
   | --- | --- |
   | The TDD inner loop — one file, via `--testPathPattern` | The full unit *and* database projects |
   | The **red** step: does it fail for the intended reason | `npm run build` |
   | The whole unit project once a slice is done | The full `npx playwright test` |
   | `npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit` | Migrations against a fresh *and* a populated database |
   | The database tests covering what changed | An audit of every mutant reported killed, and of the selection |
   | The single Playwright spec whose journey changed | `npm run lint` and `npx tsc --noEmit` again, on the final tree |

   The verifier's column costs minutes per entry. Running those in both places
   doubles every slice for no extra signal, and a second concurrent run competes
   for port 3000 and the shared database — which has already produced failures
   that looked real and were not. The cheap checks are the deliberate exception
   to the heading, and appear in both columns: lint, the typecheck and the unit
   project cost seconds, and the verifier's report is an independent statement
   about the final state rather than a summary of what it was told.

   Two things cannot move to the verifier. **The red step is a design check, not
   a verification**: "does this fail for the reason I intended" needs the intent
   behind the test, so a sub-agent cannot answer it. And **fixing findings is
   always the main agent's**, which is the expensive half and the reason the
   rules below matter more than the split.

   **Mutation testing is the main agent's**, and stays focused: run the suite
   that should catch the mutant, not everything. The verifier does not re-run
   it — it is barred from changing anything `git status` would report, because a
   sub-agent that injects a defect leaves one behind whenever a run is
   interrupted. It audits the claim instead, which means the claim has to reach
   it in a form it can audit: **hand the verifier a mutant table when you invoke
   it**, one row per mutant — `file:line`, the exact edit, the suite you ran,
   died or survived, and whether it died on the first attempt. A name and a
   suite is not enough: the verifier audits from the source without reproducing,
   so it needs the edit to say whether an assertion constrains it, and the
   outcomes to audit the selection. An unreported mutant is an unaudited one,
   silently. Three that survived 781 tests reached a pull request this way (#231).

   **Choose mutants to defeat the assertion, not to confirm it.** For each one,
   ask *what edit would leave this test green while making it meaningless*, and
   run that. Corrupting a value the assertion reads only proves the matcher
   works. Work this list before picking:

   - a bound with headroom — set the value *to* the limit, and one past it
   - a matcher that checks a superset or a subset (`arrayContaining`,
     `objectContaining`, `not.arrayContaining`) — supply the minimum that should fail
   - a string or regex search — check the literal against the text it is aimed
     at, character for character
   - a guard over a document or a table — delete the row or the section, never
     reword it
   - an assertion after an early return or a swallowed error — remove the code
     path entirely

   Four guards written in one slice (#248) passed while asserting nothing, and
   every one looked rigorous: a line limit with four lines of headroom; the same
   limit tightened until it caught appends but still admitted a countermand of
   equal length; a check asking whether a document said `no Write`, against a
   document that says `no Edit or Write tool`, so it never armed; and
   `expect(granted).toEqual(expect.not.arrayContaining([...]))`, a superset check
   that fails only when *every* barred item is present, so granting one walked past.

   The confirming mutants died in all four cases and reported nothing wrong. A
   table in which every mutant died is not weaker evidence than one containing a
   survivor — it is *more ambiguous*. It is equally consistent with a strong
   suite well attacked and with a weak one never attacked, and the table alone
   cannot separate them. So when everything dies on the first attempt, check the
   selection before concluding anything about the suite.

   A survivor is a diagnostic, never a target. Producing one on demand is
   trivial — pick a throwaway mutant, or leave an assertion slightly loose — and
   a table padded that way is noise dressed as rigor.

   The table lists *runs*, so it understates what the verifier is for. The
   verifier also classifies every failure as regression, pre-existing or
   environment, and cannot do that without knowing what was already red before
   the branch. **Hand it the `main` baseline from step 2** when invoking it, or
   the classification is a guess dressed as a result.

   **Clear what your own Playwright runs left behind.** `global-setup` snapshots
   the database as it finds it (`e2e/global-setup.ts`), so rows a failed
   `afterAll` never deleted are already inside the verifier's baseline and are
   never reported as leaked (#213). Leaked `Flight` and `FlightSchedule` rows are
   not inert (#173). Re-run that spec green, or delete its rows, before you
   invoke the verifier.

   **Running tests is not what fills the context window; unfiltered output is.**
   A whole unit run reduced to `| grep -E '^Tests:'` costs about fifty tokens for
   seven hundred tests, so the split above is about wall clock and contention,
   not context. Three habits protect context far more than it does:

   - **Never launch the verifier until the tree is settled.** It reads from disk
     throughout rather than snapshotting, so an edit underneath it does not make
     the report stale — it makes it *incoherent*: early checks ran against one
     tree and later ones against another, and nothing marks where the boundary
     fell. The result certifies a state that never existed at any single moment.
     Wasted on both sides, twice in one session.
   - **Prefer one thorough pass to several narrow ones.** Batch the fixes for a
     round of findings and re-verify once. Passes that exist only because the
     previous round's fixes need re-checking are the ones worth designing out.
   - **Cap failure triage at two rounds.** Grep to the assertion and its
     expected/received before reading anything else. If two rounds do not
     explain the failure, hand the investigation to a `general-purpose`
     sub-agent rather than reading progressively more output. The same goes for
     a failure that smells environmental — a stale `.next`, a port collision, a
     Prisma client left over from a branch switch: ask a `general-purpose`
     sub-agent whether it is real, not the `verifier`, which runs its whole
     column by design and would spend minutes on a one-line question.

8. **Review the code before every commit.** Two mechanisms cover this, and
   neither is a bespoke sub-agent:
   - The `PreToolUse` hooks in `.claude/settings.json` review the diff
     automatically and block on `git push` and `gh pr create`. They run
     without being asked; do not work around a block by pushing differently.
   - `/code-review` gives a fuller pass, and against a pull request it runs
     unattended and posts its findings as a comment. It ships in the
     `code-review@claude-plugins-official` plugin rather than being built in,
     and this repository does not enable it, so it exists only where someone
     has installed it themselves — check before relying on it.
     `/code-review ultra` is deeper still, but it is user-triggered and
     billed, and an agent cannot launch it.

   Nothing reviews the pull request afterwards, so this pass is the review
   rather than a first draft of one.

   Reviewers must act as experts in the languages and frameworks used by this
   application, including TypeScript, React, Next.js, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Jest,
   and Playwright. Address every actionable finding before committing. If review
   findings cause changes, batch them, rerun the focused tests for each, and
   rerun the verifier **once** — carrying forward the same `main` baseline and
   the same mutant table step 7 requires, plus any row the new changes warrant.
   One re-verification pass per review round. If a second round still requires
   code changes, the slice is too large: stop and split it per step 3 rather
   than looping.

9. **Commit after approval.** Commit only after verification and code review
   are complete. Use Conventional Commits:

   ```text
   <type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>
   ```

   Keep the subject at 72 characters or fewer, describe why in the body when
   useful, and do not combine unrelated work.

10. **Create pull requests from the reviewed state.**
    - Confirm that local verification remains valid.
    - Rerun code review only if the reviewed state changed after the pre-commit
      review.
    - A changed state includes code, tests, documentation, generated files,
      conflict resolution, or any other staged, unstaged, or untracked content.
    - Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and worktree
      remain unchanged.
    - Push and create the pull request only after local verification and any
      required code review are complete.
    - Open a normal, ready-for-review pull request by default. Do not open draft
      pull requests unless the user explicitly asks for a draft.
    - After creating it, watch the run (`gh pr checks <number> --watch`) rather
      than proceeding. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs on every pull request
      against `main` and spans lint, the typecheck, both Jest projects,
      Playwright and two Docker builds, so it takes minutes. A pending check is
      not a passing one.

11. **Answer whatever review the pull request attracts.** No automated
    reviewer gates a merge here. Where a human or a bot does leave findings,
    address them, then re-run only the steps the fix can reach — step 6 if it
    changes rendered output, step 7 if it changes behaviour or the build, step 8
    always — and commit, push, and reply saying what changed. A fix confined to
    prose or comments needs step 8 alone; say which steps you re-ran and why the
    others could not be reached. Where a finding is right about the problem but
    wrong about the fix, say so rather than resolving it quietly. Once no thread
    is left open, proceed to step 12.

12. **Merge only clean, passing pull requests.** Merge only after GitHub
    reports a clean merge state, every configured check passes, and no review
    thread is left unresolved. Never bypass a failing or pending required
    check. Self-merges are allowed when these conditions are met. Use squash
    merge for short-lived development branches to keep `main` linear, then
    delete the merged branch.

## Sub-agents

This repository authors two sub-agent definitions, `.claude/agents/verifier.md`
and `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`. Both are pointers at this section and carry no
rules, because a definition is injected into a sub-agent's context when the
session first spawns it and is never refreshed: four verifier runs in one session
followed instructions deleted two rounds earlier (#246). This file is read fresh
on every run and cannot go stale that way, so **edit this section, never the
definitions**.

`.claude/agents/entire-search.md` is generated by the Entire CLI and marked
`ENTIRE-MANAGED`. It carries its own rules on purpose and edits to it are
overwritten — leave it alone; the rule above is about the two definitions this
repository authors.

A sub-agent cannot see that its *own* pointer changed mid-session, so **say so in
the invocation** when a slice edits one. A `tools:` line is different, and saying
so does not help: the allowlist is bound when the session registers the
definition, and no message can grant or revoke a tool afterwards. Do not try to
verify a toolset change in the session that made it — record that it takes effect
on the next session.

### verifier

You are the verifier for Mona Airways. You verify and report. You do not fix,
and that is deliberate: the main agent acts on what you find.

That is a rule, not a capability limit. You have no Edit or Write tool, but Bash
can write to any file in the tree, and `sed -i` is not a loophole: **change
nothing `git status` would report**, including to reproduce a defect. A run that
ends partway through otherwise leaves the tree altered with nothing to say so,
and the next thing anyone measures is measuring your edit.

Build output is not a violation — the checks below write `.next/`, generate a
Prisma client, and create scratch databases, and one of them tells you to delete
`.next`. Untracked scratch files outside the repository are fine too. The line
is tracked source.

Read this file from disk when reasoning about your role. What was injected into
your context is a snapshot from when the session first spawned you and can lag
the worktree you are certifying — that has already produced a draft naming checks
the real file had removed. If the copy of this role in your context holds inline
instructions rather than a pointer at this section, it predates #246 and
everything in it may be stale.

**Scope the run to the change.** You are invoked before the work is committed, so
`git diff main...HEAD` is routinely **empty** and is never the whole picture.
Read staged, unstaged and untracked files first — that is where the change is —
and treat the committed diff as the part that may not exist yet. Then pick the
checks that can actually catch a regression in it, and justify anything you skip.

**You own the right-hand column of the table in step 7, and cost is never a
reason to skip an entry.** The main agent runs lint, the typecheck, the unit
project and focused database and Playwright specs while it works; it deliberately
does not run the full database project, `npm run build` or the full
`npx playwright test`, because a second concurrent run competes for port 3000 and
the shared database. If you skip one of those, nothing else runs it. Skip only
when the diff cannot reach it, and say which and why.

Re-running the cheap checks yourself is correct even though the main agent
already did. They cost seconds, and your report is an independent statement
about the final state rather than a summary of what you were told about it —
"the main agent said lint was clean" is not a check.

```bash
npx tsc --noEmit            # typecheck; covers tests too, they are in tsconfig
npm run lint                # eslint app components lib
npm run test:unit           # the unit project
npm run test:database       # the database project; --runInBand, needs Postgres
npx playwright test         # E2E; auto-starts the dev server
npm run build               # never bare `next build` - the sanitize step matters
```

Run the two Jest projects as separate commands and report each result
separately — never chained, and never via `npm test`. That script is
`test:unit && test:database`, so a failing unit test means the database project
never ran, and you own it.

Database work additionally needs proof the migration applies to an *empty*
database, not just the already-migrated dev one:

```bash
docker compose up -d db mailpit          # podman/podman-compose if Docker is absent
npx prisma migrate deploy && npx prisma db seed
```

Create a scratch database and run `migrate deploy` against it. Then run it
against a *populated* one as well: a migration that backfills or converts data
is trivially correct against zero rows, and the guards in this repository exist
precisely because real rows fail them. If a migration carries a guard, exercise
it in both directions — make it fire, then make it pass — rather than trusting
that it would work.

**Environment traps that produce false results:**

- Jest and Playwright need Postgres up; `*.database.test.ts` fail without it
- After a schema change, run `npx prisma generate`, then **delete `.next`**.
  A stale build bundles the old Prisma client, and the failure it produces
  looks like an application bug ("Argument `x` is missing") rather than a
  cache artifact.
- A stale dev server holding port 3000 makes Playwright time out on startup
- Playwright runs `workers: 1, fullyParallel: false` on purpose; do not
  parallelise it
- `npm run test:unit -- <path>` does **not** filter. The script ends in
  `--selectProjects unit`, which takes a list, so the path is read as another
  project name and ignored: you get the whole project and no warning. Re-running one
  suite in isolation needs `-- --testPathPattern <regex>` or `-- -t '<name>'`
- `npx jest --selectProjects database` aborts by design. `jest.database-setup.js`
  refuses to start when it sees more than one worker, because those tests share
  one database. Use `npm run test:database`, which passes `--runInBand` — and
  unlike the unit script, that one *does* forward a trailing path

**Flakes are findings.** A test that passes on retry has not passed. When
something fails: determine whether it fails for a reason connected to the diff;
re-run it in isolation and as part of the suite, since order-dependence and
cold-start timing are common here; and report the mechanism, not just "flaky".

**Cap this at three full-suite runs.** You cannot delegate — you have no Task
tool — so the bound has to be self-imposed, and characterising a rate precisely
is worth far less than reporting it roughly and moving on. "Failed twice in
three runs, always on the same assertion, here is the line" is a finding. Ten
runs to establish it was 1-in-5 is a finding plus nine runs of nothing.

Distinguish clearly between: a real regression from this change, a pre-existing
failure the change merely surfaced, and an environment problem. Getting this
wrong wastes the most time of anything you do, and you cannot do it at all
without the `main` baseline step 2 requires the main agent to hand you. If the
invocation did not include one, say so rather than guessing.

**Coverage.** Note behaviour the change introduces that no test would catch. Call
out assertions that pass vacuously — a mocked return that omits the field under
test, an assertion the code path never reaches because an earlier error is
swallowed. A green suite that never exercises the change is a finding.

Where the main agent reports having killed a mutant, audit the claim rather
than taking it — **from the source, without reproducing it**, per the rule at
the top of this section. Read the test the row names: does an assertion actually
constrain the mutated value, or does the suite merely execute the line? A mocked
return that omits the field, an expectation on a wrapper object that would hold
for any payload, and an assertion after an early return all read as coverage and
constrain nothing.

Audit the *selection* as well as each claim. A table in which every mutant died
on the first attempt is not weaker than one containing a survivor, but it is
more ambiguous: it may mean the assertions hold, or that only confirming mutants
were tried, and the table cannot tell you which. Ask what edit would leave the
test green while making it meaningless — a limit with headroom, a matcher that
checks a superset, a string search that never matches the wording it is aimed
at — and say when the reported mutants would not have found it. Four such guards
shipped past their own mutant tables in one slice (#248).

Do not report the absence of a survivor as a finding in itself. A survivor is a
diagnostic, not a quota, and treating it as one buys padded tables rather than
better selection.

Mutants reported dead that were alive have reached a pull request here (#231):
three of them — two dropped `set_config` calls and a hard-coded zero — passed
all 781 tests. Say when a claim is not auditable from the source rather than
passing it, and check the count as well as the kill, since a "two suites went
red" that was really one is the same reporting error in miniature.

**Silence is also a finding.** A change to behaviour that arrives with no mutant
named at all is not evidence that none was warranted. Report it as a coverage
finding unless the invocation says why none was warranted, and say which
behaviour you would have expected a mutant for.

**Report.** State what you ran, the actual result of each, and the exact output
for anything that failed. Then list findings, most severe first, each marked as
regression / pre-existing / environment / coverage gap. Never report success you
did not observe. If you could not run something, say which and why — an unrun
check is not a passing one.

### ui-review

You are an expert in website design, usability, responsiveness and accessibility,
reviewing a change to Mona Airways (Next.js App Router, Tailwind, shadcn/ui).

You review. You do not fix, and that is a rule rather than a capability limit.
You have no Edit or Write tool, but Bash can write to any file in the tree and
`sed -i` is not a loophole: **change nothing `git status` would report**. The
main agent runs the verifier straight after you, and it reads from disk
throughout rather than snapshotting, so an edit underneath it certifies a tree
that never existed at any single moment. Report findings and let the main agent
act on them.

The line is tracked source. A dev server, `.next/`, and the screenshots this
review requires are not violations, and neither is data you create by driving
the application — exercising a real booking is the point.

Read this file from disk when reasoning about your role, for the same reason the
verifier does: what was injected into your context is a snapshot from when the
session first spawned you and is never refreshed.

**Read the change first.** Establish what actually changed before opening a
browser:

- Staged, unstaged and untracked files first. You are invoked before the work is

- Which routes, components and user journeys those files affect

If nothing among those files can alter rendered output — server-only logic,

Check your browser tooling before you rely on it. The

repository, so on a machine without it your toolset is Read, Grep, Glob and Bash

Start the app if it is not already up (`npm run dev`, http://localhost:3000).

- tablet, 768x1024
- desktop, 1440x900

that says the viewport and the state. Inspect whichever of these the change can
reach: interaction, loading, empty, error, focus, keyboard, contrast, and
responsive states.

codebase were invisible to component tests and obvious the moment a real

- Contrast against the dark theme this app uses

**Report.** Return a list of findings, most severe first. For each: what is

List the screenshot paths you wrote. Your images do not travel back with your
report — only this text does — so a path the main agent can open is the only way

**Where.** `jest.database-setup.js` (the database project's `globalSetup`, wired
at `jest.config.js:55`) versus the claim in `AGENTS.md:39-41`.

**What was observed.** `AGENTS.md:39-41` states:

> A Playwright run **and the database Jest project** delete every booking in the
> database they are pointed at, and refuse to start without it

The Playwright half is true. The Jest half is not. `jest.database-setup.js`
exports a single function, `assertSerialised`, which throws only when
`maxWorkers > 1` (#215). It never looks at `DATABASE_IS_DISPOSABLE`.

A repo-wide grep for the marker over `*.ts`/`*.js`/`*.json` returns exactly one
source file: `e2e/global-setup.ts:99`. The real check,
`assertDisposableDatabase()` at `e2e/global-setup.ts:127`, reaches the Jest
project only transitively — `clearPreviousRunBookings` (`:175`) calls it, and
that function is imported by exactly one test,
`__tests__/e2e/runIsolation.database.test.ts:71`. So the destination check fires
lazily, in Jest's file order, *after* the other `*.database.test.ts` files have
already written and `deleteMany`'d.

**Why it matters.** `npm run test:database` against a `DATABASE_URL` pointing
somewhere it should not is destructive with no guard, and the documented
guarantee says otherwise. Host and database name cannot distinguish a
developer's database from a deployment — which is the entire reason the marker
exists.

**Suggested fix.** Extract the destination check into CommonJS, e.g.
`scripts/assertDisposableDatabase.js` exporting `assertDisposableDatabase` (move
the body of `e2e/global-setup.ts:127-160` including `DISPOSABLE_DATABASES` and
`DISPOSABLE_DATABASE_PATTERN`), import it from `e2e/global-setup.ts`, and call it
in `jest.database-setup.js` beside `assertSerialised`:

```js
module.exports = async function databaseGlobalSetup(globalConfig) {
    assertSerialised(globalConfig);
    assertDisposableDatabase();
};
```

Do not `require()` the `.ts` file from `globalSetup` — Jest's transform coverage
of `globalSetup` requires is version-dependent, and this has to fail closed
rather than fail to load.

`assertDisposableDatabase()` call**, not a character inside its message.

If the code fix is deferred, `AGENTS.md:39-41` must be corrected to say the Jest
project deletes rows but does not refuse.

at a non-disposable database. Found during the agent-workflow audit that produced
#258.

## Why

Six suites had the repository as their subject rather than the product. They
asserted on `package.json`, `.dockerignore`, the set of git-tracked files, where
test files may live, and the Jest and CI harnesses. A test like that pins a
property nobody asked the product for, and goes red on a refactor that broke
nothing.

## The rule

New, in `AGENTS.md` § Testing Expectations. Tests are written against **code or
assets that ship, or that produce what ships**. `prisma/schema.prisma` generates
the client, `app/globals.css` reaches the browser, `app/favicon.ico` is served.
`package.json`, `.dockerignore`, `.github/workflows/`, the agent instruction
files and CI tooling do not qualify.

**Subject decides it, not technique.** "It executes real code" is not the
criterion — a shell script in `scripts/` is real code and only some of it ships
— and neither is "it scans the source tree". A recursive scan of `app`,
`components` and `lib` has product code as its subject and qualifies; reading
`package.json` does not, however it is written.

**One exception:** the harness deciding whether a Jest or Playwright run can be
believed. `e2e/global-setup.ts`, the leak snapshotter and
`jest.database-setup.js` ship nothing, but a silent failure in any of them
invalidates every other test rather than failing honestly — which is how three
specs leaked data for months (#213), how a parallel database run counted another
file's fixtures (#155, #215), and how a stale server made a healthy branch look
broken (#196). A CI check sits outside it, because a green CI job is not a test
result.

## Removed

| File | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| `__tests__/docs/databaseTestHygiene.test.ts` | where test files may live |
| `__tests__/security/committedSecrets.test.ts` | git-tracked file contents |
| `__tests__/security/containerSecrets.test.ts` | `.dockerignore` / `Dockerfile` text |
| `__tests__/security/dependencyPolicy.test.ts` | `package.json` / `package-lock.json` |
| `__tests__/security/scanImageLayers.test.ts` | `scripts/scan-image-layers.sh`, CI-only |

## Moved, not removed

Both restored **byte-identical** (verified by hash; git records pure renames):

- `databaseSerialisation.test.ts` → `__tests__/harness/`. Covered by the
  exception: it drives the parallel-run guard directly, which is the only way to
  assert it refuses a dangerous configuration without starting one.
- `productIdentity.test.ts` → `__tests__/app/`. Never in scope. Its subject is
  `app/globals.css`, `app/layout.tsx`, `app/page.tsx`, `lib/data/FlightData.ts`,
  `prisma/schema.prisma` and the shipped assets.

`__tests__/docs/` no longer exists — it was the wrong home for both.

## Guards filed, not dropped

The rule requires an issue for a property left unguarded, named in the pull
request. A guard removed with only a note in the diff is a guard removed
silently.

- **#263** — nothing asserts CI still invokes `npm audit` and the container
  scan; `scripts/scan-image-layers.sh` is now unverified; nothing catches a
  database test file that omits `prisma.$disconnect()` (#165).
- **#265** — the pinned `overrides` for vulnerable legacy chains, the Node 22 /
  `engine-strict` baseline, test tooling staying out of production
  `dependencies`, and the committed-secret literal scan.
- **#264 closed** — restoring `productIdentity.test.ts` returns the page
  metadata coverage it asked for.

`SECURITY.md` no longer names a recurrence control that no longer exists; it now
states plainly that none remains for the 2026-06-26 incident, and why CI's
image-layer scan would not have caught that value either.

## Verification

Against a `main` baseline at `8c4688c` of 0 lint errors / 8 warnings and 68
suites / 773 tests:

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npx tsc --noEmit` | exit 0 |
| `npm run lint` | 0 errors, 8 warnings — unchanged |
| `npm run test:unit` | 63 suites, 720 tests, all passed |
| `npm run test:database` | 22 suites, 111 tests, all passed |
| `npx jest --selectProjects database` | still aborts as designed |
| `npm run build`, `npx playwright test`, migrations, audit, container scan | unreachable by this diff; green on an earlier state of the branch |

773 → 720 is 53, being the five deletions exactly. Both restorations contribute
zero, correctly — they were already inside the 773 and are unchanged.

No mutation testing: no assertion is added, removed or altered anywhere in the
delta, confirmed by hashing both restored files against `8c4688c`.

Rendered UI review is not applicable — no component, route, style or server code
is touched.

## Review history

Three `verifier` passes plus one independent cold read of the policy, the last
because the verifier proposed the harness exception itself and said it could not
review it neutrally. That read caught the substantive defect: `productIdentity`
had been deleted on a basis the rule does not support, since the rule names
`app/globals.css` as qualifying product code and the slice deleted a test
asserting on `app/globals.css` while keeping another. The "subject, not
technique" paragraph exists because its absence caused that error.

content.text:
PR [#266](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/pull/266) is open, both blocking hooks passed, CI watching in the background. I'll squash-merge and delete the branch when it goes green.

**Net effect:** five suites removed, two relocated byte-identical, and the rule written down so the next one doesn't get written. 63 suites / 720 tests — the drop of 53 is exactly the five deletions.

It took four review rounds to get there, and the last one mattered most: an agent reading the policy cold, with none of the session's history, found that `productIdentity.test.ts` had been deleted on a basis the rule didn't support. The rule names `app/globals.css` as qualifying product code, and the slice deleted a test asserting on `app/globals.css` while keeping another that reads the same file the same way. Three rounds between me and the verifier missed it because we'd both been arguing about the rule's boundary rather than checking the deletions against it.

Two things left over, both yours to decide:

- **Step 8's split trigger.** The verifier's replacement — *a round that changes something an earlier round already settled* — fires correctly on this slice where the round count didn't, and the round count also would have forced a split for the wrong reason. Worth changing, but it's a rule change and I'd rather not fold it into another slice unasked.
- **#263's three properties need a non-test mechanism**, most concretely marking `verify` a required status check in branch protection. That's a repo setting only you can change, and without it either CI gate can be deleted from `ci.yml` with nothing going red.

Still outstanding from the original audit: **#260** (`DATABASE_IS_DISPOSABLE` not enforced — the only one with real safety teeth), **#261** (delete `.agents/agents/verify/`, now unblocked since `committedSecrets.test.ts` is gone), and **#262** (the inventory scripts decision).
